title: German
description: A practical first course in German for absolute beginners who want to actually speak and understand the language. You will master pronunciation features like umlauts and the sharp s, the core grammar patterns, including gender, case, and verb-second word order, that carry most everyday speech, and the vocabulary for real situations like meeting people, describing your family, ordering food, shopping, and talking about the past.
outcomes: You can pronounce German umlauts, the sharp s (ß), the two ch-sounds, and understand final-consonant devoicing.
You can greet people, introduce yourself, and use sein and haben correctly for identity, location, possession, and idioms like age and hunger.
You can build correct noun phrases with proper gender, plural forms, nominative/accusative articles, and possessive articles.
You can conjugate regular and common stem-changing verbs in the present tense, apply verb-second word order, and form questions and negation with nicht or kein.
You can handle real situations — ordering food, shopping, asking directions — using numbers, time expressions, and everyday vocabulary.
You can describe a completed past event using the Perfekt tense, choosing correctly between haben and sein as the auxiliary.

units.title: Sounds and Greetings
units.summary: German spelling is consistent once you learn its distinctive sounds, like umlauts and the sharp s. This unit builds the pronunciation and greeting toolkit for a first real conversation.

lessons.title: German Pronunciation Basics
lessons.intro: German spelling is remarkably consistent once you learn a few sound rules, but three features, umlauts, the ß, and the two ch-sounds, need explicit attention since English has nothing quite like them.

sections.heading: Umlauts: ä, ö, ü
body: The umlaut (two dots) changes a vowel's sound entirely: *ä* is like the 'e' in 'bed,' *ö* is like the vowel in French 'fleur' or English 'her' said with rounded lips, and *ü* is like French 'tu,' made by saying 'ee' with rounded lips. These aren't decorations; *schon* (already) and *schön* (beautiful) are completely different words distinguished only by the umlaut.

Umlauts also do grammatical work: many nouns add an umlaut to their vowel when forming the plural, alongside or instead of an ending — *der Bruder* (brother) becomes *die Brüder* (brothers), and *die Mutter* (mother) becomes *die Mütter* (mothers), with no added ending at all beyond the umlaut.

sections.heading: The Sharp S: ß
body: *ß* (called *Eszett* or *scharfes S*) represents a sharp, unvoiced 's' sound and appears after a long vowel or diphthong: *Straße* (street), *groß* (big). Where the vowel before is short, a double *ss* is used instead: *Fluss* (river), *dass* (that, conjunction).
In Switzerland, ß is not used at all; ss replaces it everywhere. Elsewhere, whether a word takes ß or ss is largely determined by vowel length, which makes it learnable rather than arbitrary.

sections.heading: Two Sounds for CH, and W vs V
body: *Ch* has two distinct sounds: after *e* and *i*, it's a soft, breathy hiss at the front of the mouth (the *ich-Laut*, as in *ich*, I); after *a, o, u*, it's a harsher, back-of-throat rasp (the *ach-Laut*, as in *ach*, an exclamation). *W* is pronounced like English 'v' (*Wasser*, water, sounds like 'VAH-ser'), while *v* is pronounced like English 'f' (*Vater*, father, sounds like 'FAH-ter').

Final consonants also devoice: a b, d, or g at the very end of a word is pronounced like p, t, or k. *Hund* (dog) sounds like 'hoont,' not 'hoond' — this devoicing is completely regular and applies to every word ending this way.

example.problem: Given that ß follows a long vowel/diphthong and ss follows a short vowel, would 'groß' (big) and 'Fluss' (river) use ß or ss? And how does 'Hund' (dog) actually sound when spoken?
steps: Groß has a long o sound, so it takes ß: groß.
Fluss has a short u sound, so it takes ss: Fluss.
Hund ends in d, which devoices to a t-sound at the end of a word: pronounced 'hoont.'
example.answer: groß (long vowel → ß) and Fluss (short vowel → ss); Hund is pronounced 'hoont' due to final-consonant devoicing.

keyTerms.def: The two dots over ä, ö, ü that change a vowel's sound and often mark plural forms.
The sharp-s letter used after a long vowel or diphthong, as in Straße and groß.
The two ch sounds: a soft hiss after e/i (ich) and a harsher rasp after a/o/u (ach).
The rule that b, d, and g sound like p, t, and k at the very end of a German word, as in Hund → 'hoont.'

practice.q: What does the umlaut in 'schön' (beautiful) do compared to 'schon' (already)?
choices: Changes the vowel sound, creating a different word entirely
practice.explain: Umlauts change the vowel sound; schön and schon are distinct, unrelated words that happen to differ only by the umlaut.

practice.q: Which word would correctly use ß rather than ss?
practice.explain: ß follows a long vowel or diphthong, as in groß; Fluss, dass, and Schloss all have short vowels and take ss.

practice.q: How is 'Hund' (dog) pronounced at the end of the word?
choices: Like 'hoont,' with the d devoiced to t
practice.explain: Final b/d/g devoice to p/t/k in German, so Hund is pronounced 'hoont,' not 'hoond.'

lessons.title: Greetings and Introductions
lessons.intro: German greetings shift by time of day, and, just like Spanish and French, the du/Sie choice you make in your very first sentence sets the tone for the whole relationship.

sections.heading: Hello and Goodbye
body: *Guten Morgen* (good morning) covers the early hours, *Guten Tag* (good day) is the safe default from late morning through afternoon, and *Guten Abend* (good evening) takes over in the evening. *Hallo* (hi) is casual and works nearly anywhere, any time.

To say goodbye, *Auf Wiedersehen* is the standard formal choice; *Tschüss* is warm and casual, used constantly among friends and colleagues. In southern Germany and Austria, *Servus* can mean both 'hi' and 'bye.'

sections.heading: Introducing Yourself
body: To give your name, say *Ich heiße* + name (literally 'I am called'), as in *Ich heiße Anna*. Ask informally with *Wie heißt du?* or formally with *Wie heißen Sie?* You can also say *Ich bin* + name (*Ich bin Anna*, 'I am Anna'), using the verb sein covered next.

To ask how someone is doing, use *Wie geht es dir?* (informal) or *Wie geht es Ihnen?* (formal); a common reply is *Mir geht es gut, danke* (I'm doing well, thanks) — the person feeling well appears as mir/dir/Ihnen, not as the grammatical subject, an early hint of how German cases work.

sections.heading: Du vs Sie
body: German has *du* (informal 'you,' for friends, family, children, and peers) and *Sie* (formal 'you,' always capitalized, for strangers, elders, and professional contexts — also used for both singular and plural formal address). Sie is grammatically identical in form to the third-person plural 'they' (sie, lowercase), so capitalization is the only way to tell them apart in writing.

As in Spanish and French, defaulting to Sie with anyone new is always safe, and switching to du generally waits for an explicit invitation, often phrased as *Wollen wir uns duzen?* (Shall we use 'du' with each other?).

example.problem: You're meeting your German landlord for the first time. How do you greet them and ask their name, using the correct formality?
steps: This is a formal, unfamiliar context, so use Sie.
Greet with Guten Tag.
Ask: Wie heißen Sie?
example.answer: Guten Tag, wie heißen Sie? — using Sie because the situation is formal and you don't yet know this person.

keyTerms.def: Good day, the safe default German greeting from late morning through afternoon.
'I am called' / 'My name is,' the standard way to introduce yourself in German.
The informal singular 'you,' used with friends, family, and peers.
The formal 'you' (singular or plural), always capitalized, used with strangers and in professional contexts.

practice.q: How is 'Sie' (formal you) distinguished in writing from 'sie' (they)?
choices: There is no difference at all
practice.explain: Formal Sie and third-person plural sie are identical in form; only the capital S signals the formal 'you.'

practice.q: What is the informal way to ask 'How are you?'
practice.explain: Wie geht es dir? uses the informal dir; the formal version is Wie geht es Ihnen?

practice.q: What signals it's appropriate to switch from Sie to du?
choices: An explicit invitation, such as 'Wollen wir uns duzen?'
There is no such signal in German
practice.explain: Switching from Sie to du in German typically waits for an explicit mutual agreement, just as with vous/tu in French.

lessons.title: Sein and Haben: The Two Essential Verbs
lessons.intro: Sein (to be) and haben (to have) are both irregular, appear in nearly every sentence, and later combine with a past participle to build Germany's everyday past tense.

sections.heading: Sein: To Be
body: Sein conjugates as: *ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind*. Like French être, sein alone covers identity, description, and location, with no separate ser/estar-style split: *Ich bin müde* (I am tired), *Das Buch ist auf dem Tisch* (The book is on the table).

Sein is also the auxiliary used to build the perfect past tense for verbs of motion and change of state, a pattern covered later in this course — a strong hint of how central this one verb is to the whole language.

sections.heading: Haben: To Have
body: Haben conjugates as: *ich habe, du hast, er/sie/es hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben*. Beyond possession (*ich habe einen Hund*, I have a dog), haben appears in idioms where English uses 'to be': *Hunger haben* (to be hungry, literally 'to have hunger'), *Angst haben* (to be afraid).

*Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt* (I am twenty years old) actually uses sein, not haben, for age in German — the opposite pattern from Spanish and French, which both use their 'to have' verb for age. This is a common point of confusion for learners coming from a Romance language.

example.problem: Say 'I am hungry and I am 25 years old' in German, choosing the correct verb for each part.
steps: 'Hungry' is a haben idiom: ich habe Hunger.
Age in German uses sein, not haben: ich bin fünfundzwanzig Jahre alt.
Combine with und (and): Ich habe Hunger und ich bin fünfundzwanzig Jahre alt.
example.answer: Ich habe Hunger und ich bin fünfundzwanzig Jahre alt.

keyTerms.def: 'To be'; covers identity, description, and location, and is also used for age in German.
'To have'; used for possession and idioms like Hunger haben (to be hungry) and Angst haben (to be afraid).
German states age with sein (ich bin ... Jahre alt), unlike Spanish and French, which use their 'to have' verb.
The idiom 'to have hunger,' meaning 'to be hungry.'

practice.q: How do you say 'I am 20 years old' in German?
practice.explain: German states age with sein: ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt, unlike Spanish/French which use their 'to have' verb.

practice.q: What does 'Angst haben' mean?
practice.explain: Angst haben literally means 'to have fear,' the standard idiom for 'to be afraid'; Hunger haben means 'to be hungry.'

practice.q: Which verb does German use to build the perfect past tense for motion verbs?
practice.explain: Sein serves as the auxiliary for verbs of motion and change of state in the German perfect tense, a pattern covered later in the course.

units.title: Nouns, Gender, and Cases
units.summary: Every German noun is capitalized and carries a gender, and its article shifts depending on its grammatical case. This unit builds the noun-phrase skills used in every sentence from here on.

lessons.title: Gender and Plural of Nouns
lessons.intro: Every German noun is capitalized, always, and carries one of three genders — a system with fewer shortcuts than Spanish or French, but a handful of patterns still help.

sections.heading: Der, Die, Das
body: German has three genders: *der* (masculine), *die* (feminine), *das* (neuter), all meaning 'the' in the singular; the plural definite article is *die* for every gender. *Der Mann* (the man), *die Frau* (the woman), *das Kind* (the child), *die Kinder* (the children).

One famous surprise: *das Mädchen* (the girl) is grammatically neuter, not feminine, because any noun ending in the diminutive suffix *-chen* or *-lein* is automatically neuter, regardless of the person's actual gender. This overrides what you might expect from meaning alone.

sections.heading: Some Gender Patterns
body: A few endings do predict gender reliably: words ending in *-ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft* are always feminine (*die Zeitung* newspaper, *die Freiheit* freedom, *die Freundschaft* friendship). Words ending in *-chen* or *-lein* are always neuter, as just noted.

Beyond these patterns, gender mostly has to be memorized noun by noun, along with its article — the same strategy needed for French. Plurals have several patterns (add -e, -er, -n, -s, or nothing, sometimes with an umlaut), so the plural, like the gender, is usually learned together with the noun.

example.problem: What is the gender of 'das Mädchen' (the girl), and why doesn't it match the expected feminine gender?
steps: Mädchen ends in the diminutive suffix -chen.
Any noun ending in -chen or -lein is automatically grammatically neuter.
This grammatical rule overrides the natural gender of the person described, so das Mädchen is neuter despite referring to a girl.
example.answer: Das Mädchen is neuter because nouns ending in -chen are always neuter by German grammar rules, regardless of the natural gender of what they describe.

keyTerms.def: The three German definite articles: der (masc.), die (fem.), das (neuter); die also serves as the plural for all genders.
Diminutive endings that make a noun automatically neuter, as in das Mädchen (the girl).
-ung, -heit, -keit, and -schaft reliably signal a feminine noun, like die Freiheit.
A plural formed partly or entirely by adding an umlaut to the noun's vowel, as in Mutter → Mütter.

practice.q: Why is 'das Mädchen' (the girl) grammatically neuter?
choices: It ends in the diminutive suffix -chen, which is always neuter
Girls are considered neuter in German culture
Mädchen is actually feminine, and das is a typo
practice.explain: Any noun ending in -chen or -lein is automatically neuter in German grammar, regardless of the natural gender of the thing described.

practice.q: Which ending reliably signals a feminine noun?
practice.explain: -heit (like -ung, -keit, and -schaft) is a reliable feminine ending, as in die Freiheit (freedom).

practice.q: What is the plural definite article for all three genders?
practice.explain: Regardless of a noun's singular gender, the plural definite article is always die: die Kinder, die Männer, die Frauen.

lessons.title: The Nominative and Accusative Cases
lessons.intro: German nouns change form depending on their grammatical role in the sentence, a system called case, and the good news for beginners is that only the masculine article actually changes between the two most common cases.

sections.heading: What a Case Does
body: German has four cases: nominative (the subject), accusative (the direct object), dative (the indirect object), and genitive (possession). This course focuses on nominative and accusative, since together they cover the large majority of simple sentences, while noting that dative and genitive exist for later study.
The nominative case marks whoever or whatever performs the action: *Der Mann sieht den Hund* (The man sees the dog) — Mann is the subject, so it stays in the nominative (der).

sections.heading: The Accusative Case
body: The accusative marks the direct object, the thing receiving the action. Crucially, only the masculine definite article changes from nominative to accusative: *der → den*. Feminine, neuter, and plural articles stay exactly the same: *die → die*, *das → das*, *die (pl.) → die (pl.)*.

So in *Der Mann sieht den Hund* (The man sees the dog), Hund is masculine, and its article shifts from der to den because it's the direct object. But *Der Mann sieht die Frau* (The man sees the woman) shows no change at all, since die is feminine and doesn't shift in the accusative.

example.problem: In the sentence 'Ich sehe den Ball' (I see the ball, der Ball), why does 'der' become 'den'?
steps: Ball is the direct object of sehen (to see), so it takes the accusative case.
Ball is masculine (der Ball), and only masculine nouns change their article in the accusative.
Der becomes den: Ich sehe den Ball.
example.answer: Der becomes den because Ball is masculine and functions as the direct object (accusative case) in this sentence.

keyTerms.def: The grammatical role a noun plays in a sentence (subject, direct object, etc.), marked in German by changes to its article.
The case for the subject of a sentence, the one performing the action.
The case for the direct object, the thing receiving the action; only the masculine article changes (der → den).
Feminine, neuter, and plural definite articles, which stay the same in both nominative and accusative.

practice.q: Which article changes between nominative and accusative?
practice.explain: Of the four German articles, only the masculine der shifts to den in the accusative; feminine, neuter, and plural stay the same.

practice.q: In 'Der Hund sieht die Katze' (The dog sees the cat), which noun is in the accusative?
choices: die Katze (the cat), the direct object
practice.explain: Katze is the direct object of sehen, so it's in the accusative case; since Katze is feminine, its article (die) doesn't change from the nominative form.

practice.q: What does the accusative case mark?
choices: The direct object receiving the action
practice.explain: The accusative marks the direct object; the nominative marks the subject, and possession is marked by the genitive case.

lessons.title: Personal Pronouns and Possessive Articles
lessons.intro: German possessive words (mein, dein, sein...) follow the same der/die/das gender pattern you've just learned, so mastering them is mostly a matter of applying rules you already know.

sections.heading: Personal Pronouns
body: German subject pronouns are: *ich* (I), *du* (you, informal), *er/sie/es* (he/she/it), *wir* (we), *ihr* (you all, informal), *sie/Sie* (they/you, formal). Unlike Spanish, German does not typically drop the subject pronoun; it's required in almost every sentence.

*Es* (it) is used not just for objects but also for das-gender nouns referring to people, like *das Mädchen*: *Es ist klug* (She/it is smart) is grammatically correct when referring back to das Mädchen, even though the girl is a 'she' in meaning.

sections.heading: Possessive Articles
body: Possessive articles work like ein/eine, changing endings to match the gender and number of the noun owned, not the owner: *mein* (my, masc./neut.), *meine* (my, fem./plural). *Mein Bruder* (my brother, masc.), *meine Schwester* (my sister, fem.), *mein Kind* (my child, neut.).

The same pattern extends to other owners: *dein/deine* (your, informal), *sein/seine* (his), *ihr/ihre* (her/their), *unser/unsere* (our), *euer/eure* (your all), *Ihr/Ihre* (your, formal). Note that *ihr* covers both 'her' and 'their' — context tells them apart.

example.problem: Say 'My brother is tall and my sister is smart' in German, using the correct possessive for each.
steps: Bruder is masculine, so use mein: mein Bruder.
Schwester is feminine, so use meine: meine Schwester.
Combine: Mein Bruder ist groß und meine Schwester ist klug.
example.answer: Mein Bruder ist groß und meine Schwester ist klug.

keyTerms.def: A word like ich, du, or sie that identifies who performs the verb's action; required in nearly every German sentence.
'My,' agreeing with the gender and number of the noun owned, like ein/eine.
Can mean either 'her' or 'their,' depending on context, since both share the same possessive form.
'It,' also correctly used for das-gender nouns referring to people, like das Mädchen.

practice.q: Which possessive correctly means 'my sister' (die Schwester)?
practice.explain: Schwester is feminine, so the possessive takes the feminine ending: meine Schwester.

practice.q: What can 'ihr' mean, depending on context?
practice.explain: Ihr (lowercase) can mean either 'her' or 'their'; only context distinguishes them, similar to French son/sa.

practice.q: Does German typically allow you to drop the subject pronoun, like Spanish does?
choices: No, German requires the subject pronoun in almost every sentence
practice.explain: Unlike Spanish, German verb endings don't uniquely identify the subject, so the pronoun is required in nearly every sentence.

units.title: Numbers, Time, and Family
units.summary: This unit adds the vocabulary that lets you handle dates, schedules, and describing the people closest to you, plus German's reversed number order.

lessons.title: Numbers 0-100
lessons.intro: German numbers have one quirk that trips up almost every beginner: from 21 onward, the units digit is said before the tens digit, the reverse of English order.

sections.heading: Zero to Twenty
body: Zero through twelve are individual words: *null, eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn, elf, zwölf*. From thirteen to nineteen, numbers add *-zehn* (a form of 'ten') to the base: *dreizehn* (13), *vierzehn* (14), *fünfzehn* (15), *sechzehn* (16, note the dropped s), *siebzehn* (17, note the dropped en), *achtzehn* (18), *neunzehn* (19). *Zwanzig* (20) starts a new base.
These teen numbers are entirely regular in structure (base + zehn), with just two minor spelling contractions (sechzehn, siebzehn) worth noting so you're not thrown off by them.

sections.heading: Twenty-One and Beyond: Reversed Order
body: From 21 onward, German says the units digit first, then 'and,' then the tens digit, all as one word: *einundzwanzig* (21, literally 'one-and-twenty'), *zweiundzwanzig* (22), *dreiundzwanzig* (23). This reversed order continues at every ten: *einunddreißig* (31), *einundvierzig* (41), and so on.

The tens themselves are *zwanzig* (20), *dreißig* (30), *vierzig* (40), *fünfzig* (50), *sechzig* (60), *siebzig* (70), *achtzig* (80), *neunzig* (90), and *hundert* (100) — all regular once you know zwanzig.

example.problem: How do you say 47 and 82 in German?
steps: 47: units digit first (sieben, 7) + und + tens (vierzig, 40): siebenundvierzig.
82: units digit first (zwei, 2) + und + tens (achtzig, 80): zweiundachtzig.

keyTerms.def: The German pattern of saying the units digit before the tens digit from 21 onward, joined by und (and): einundzwanzig.
The suffix meaning 'teen,' attached to base numbers for 13-19: dreizehn, vierzehn.
The suffix for the tens from 20-90: zwanzig, dreißig, vierzig.
100, the clean word after the tens system resolves.

practice.q: How do you say 34 in German?
practice.explain: German reverses the order from 21 up: units first, then und, then tens: vier-und-dreißig (four-and-thirty).

practice.q: Which number is 'einundzwanzig'?
practice.explain: Einundzwanzig literally means 'one-and-twenty,' i.e., 21, following the reversed-order pattern.

practice.q: What does '-zehn' signal in a German number word?
practice.explain: -zehn is attached to base numbers to form 13-19 (dreizehn, vierzehn...); -zig forms the tens (20-90) instead.

lessons.title: Telling Time and Days/Months
lessons.intro: German time-telling has a genuinely tricky quirk at the half-hour mark that catches nearly every learner off guard at least once, worth learning carefully now rather than misreading a schedule later.

sections.heading: Asking and Telling Time
body: To ask the time, say *Wie spät ist es?* or *Wie viel Uhr ist es?* For the hour, say *Es ist ein Uhr* (It's 1:00), *Es ist zwei Uhr* (It's 2:00). For a quarter past, use *Viertel nach*: *Es ist Viertel nach drei* (3:15). For a quarter to, use *Viertel vor*: *Es ist Viertel vor vier* (3:45).

The half-hour is the genuine trap: *Es ist halb drei* does NOT mean 'half past two' — it means 'half toward three,' i.e., 2:30. German counts the half hour toward the upcoming hour, the opposite of how English speakers instinctively read 'half three.'

sections.heading: Days and Months
body: The days are *Montag, Dienstag, Mittwoch, Donnerstag, Freitag, Samstag* (or *Sonnabend* in parts of the north/east), *Sonntag* — and unlike Spanish and French, German capitalizes all of these, since they're nouns. The months are *Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai, Juni, Juli, August, September, Oktober, November, Dezember*, also capitalized.
To say 'on' a day, German uses *am* (a contraction of an + dem): *am Montag* (on Monday). For repeated habits, add -s: *montags* (on Mondays, every week), lowercase, functioning as an adverb.

example.problem: What time is 'Es ist halb sechs,' and how would you say 'on Fridays' as a weekly habit?
steps: Halb sechs means 'half toward six,' i.e., 30 minutes before six.
That is 5:30.
'On Fridays' as a habit adds -s to the day: freitags.
example.answer: Es ist halb sechs = 5:30. 'On Fridays' (habit) = freitags.

keyTerms.def: 'What time is it?' — the standard way to ask the time in German.
'Half past two' in meaning but literally 'half toward three'; German counts the half hour toward the next hour.
'Quarter past' / 'quarter to,' used for :15 and :45.
'On Mondays' (a repeated habit), formed by adding -s to the day name, lowercase.

practice.q: What time does 'Es ist halb neun' refer to?
practice.explain: Halb neun means 'half toward nine,' i.e., halfway to nine o'clock, which is 8:30 — a common trap for English speakers.

practice.q: How do you say 'quarter to four'?
practice.explain: Viertel vor means 'quarter to,' so Viertel vor vier is 3:45; Viertel nach vier would be 4:15.

practice.q: Why are German day and month names capitalized, unlike in Spanish and French?
choices: Because all German nouns are capitalized
They're actually not capitalized in German
practice.explain: German capitalizes every noun, including day and month names, unlike Spanish and French which keep them lowercase.

lessons.title: Family Vocabulary and Descriptions
lessons.intro: Family talk is the perfect place to combine gender, cases, and possessive articles into natural sentences about people who actually matter to you.

sections.heading: Family Words
body: Core vocabulary: *die Mutter* (mother), *der Vater* (father), *die Eltern* (parents, always plural), *der Bruder/die Schwester* (brother/sister), *die Großeltern* (grandparents), *der Sohn/die Tochter* (son/daughter), *der Onkel/die Tante* (uncle/aunt), *der Cousin/die Cousine* (cousin), *der Mann/die Frau* (husband/wife — these words also mean 'man' and 'woman' generally).

Notice several plurals take an umlaut shift: *die Mutter → die Mütter* (mothers), *der Bruder → die Brüder* (brothers), while *die Tochter → die Töchter* (daughters) follows the same umlaut-only pattern with no added ending.

sections.heading: Describing Family Members
body: Common descriptive adjectives: *groß* (tall), *klein* (short), *dünn* (thin), *nett* (nice), *intelligent* (smart), *jung* (young), *alt* (old). Unlike Spanish and French, German predicate adjectives (after sein) don't change form at all for gender or number: *Er ist groß*, *Sie ist groß*, *Sie sind groß* all use the same unchanged groß.

Adjectives only take endings when placed directly before the noun they describe, a case-and-gender-dependent pattern studied at a more advanced level; for now, predicate adjectives after sein stay refreshingly simple and unchanged.

example.problem: Say 'My grandfather is old but very nice' in German, using sein and the correct possessive.
steps: 'My grandfather' = mein Großvater (masculine, so mein not meine).
Predicate adjectives after sein don't change form: alt and sehr nett stay as written.
Combine with aber (but): Mein Großvater ist alt, aber sehr nett.
example.answer: Mein Großvater ist alt, aber sehr nett.

keyTerms.def: 'The parents,' a noun that exists only in the plural in German.
Several family nouns form their plural with an umlaut shift alone, like Mutter → Mütter.
An adjective following sein, which stays unchanged regardless of gender or number: Er/Sie/Sie sind groß.
Words meaning both 'husband/wife' and, more generally, 'man/woman.'

practice.q: What is the plural of 'die Mutter' (the mother)?
practice.explain: Mutter forms its plural with an umlaut shift alone, no added ending: Mutter → Mütter.

practice.q: Does the predicate adjective in 'Sie ist groß' (she is tall) change if the subject is plural, 'Sie sind groß' (they are tall)?
choices: No, groß stays exactly the same
practice.explain: Predicate adjectives following sein never change form for gender or number in German, unlike attributive adjectives placed before a noun.

practice.q: What does 'die Eltern' mean, and how is it used?
choices: 'The parents'; it exists only in the plural
'The elders'; can be singular or plural
practice.explain: Eltern means 'parents' and has no ordinary singular form in German, unlike the separate, rarer word Elternteil (one parent).

units.title: Present-Tense Verbs and Word Order
units.summary: With regular verb patterns and German's strict verb-second word order in hand, you can describe daily routines and have real back-and-forth conversations.

lessons.title: Regular Verbs and Verb-Second Word Order
lessons.intro: German verb endings are refreshingly regular for most verbs, but German word order has one strict rule, verb-second, that changes how you build every single sentence.

sections.heading: Regular Present-Tense Endings
body: To conjugate a regular verb like *machen* (to do/make), drop -en and add: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en: *ich mache, du machst, er/sie/es macht, wir machen, ihr macht, sie/Sie machen*. This exact pattern applies to hundreds of verbs: *spielen* (to play), *lernen* (to learn), *wohnen* (to live/reside).
Notice ich and sie/Sie (plural/formal) share -en-based forms with wir, while du and er/sie/es have their own distinct -st/-t endings, a pattern that becomes automatic with practice.

sections.heading: Verb-Second (V2) Word Order
body: German's most important word-order rule: the conjugated verb is always the second grammatical element in a main clause, no matter what comes first. *Ich spiele heute Fußball* (I play soccer today) puts ich first and spiele second, as expected.

But start the sentence differently, and the verb still stays second: *Heute spiele ich Fußball* (Today I play soccer, literally 'Today play I soccer') — heute takes the first slot, so spiele must move to second, pushing ich after the verb. This inversion, unfamiliar to English speakers, is completely regular and required whenever anything other than the subject opens the sentence.

example.problem: Rearrange 'Ich lerne heute Deutsch' (I learn German today) to start with 'heute' instead, keeping the verb in second position.
steps: Move heute to the front of the sentence.
The verb lerne must remain in the second position.
Ich moves after the verb: Heute lerne ich Deutsch.
example.answer: Heute lerne ich Deutsch (Today I learn German) — the verb stays second even though the sentence no longer starts with the subject.

keyTerms.def: The present-tense pattern for regular German verbs: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en.
The rule that the conjugated verb always occupies the second position in a German main clause.
The reordering of subject and verb that occurs when a word other than the subject opens the sentence, to keep the verb in second position.
An independent sentence, where the V2 rule for verb placement applies.

practice.q: In 'Heute spiele ich Fußball,' why does 'ich' come after the verb?
choices: Because heute occupies first position, and the verb must stay second
Because ich is always placed after Fußball
Because spielen is an irregular verb
There's no rule; word order is free in German
practice.explain: German's verb-second rule requires the conjugated verb to be the second element; since heute takes the first slot, ich is pushed after the verb.

practice.q: What is the 'du' ending for regular verbs?
practice.explain: The du ending for regular verbs is -st: machen → du machst.

practice.q: Which rule governs where the conjugated verb goes in a German main clause?
choices: Verb-second (V2): the verb is always the second element
Verb-final: the verb always comes last
Verb-first: the verb always starts the sentence
practice.explain: German main clauses follow verb-second word order — the conjugated verb is the second grammatical element, regardless of what comes first.

lessons.title: Stem-Changing Verbs and Common Irregulars
lessons.intro: A distinctive group of German verbs change their stem vowel only in the du and er/sie/es forms — spot this pattern once and dozens of common verbs become predictable.

sections.heading: The Stem-Vowel Change
body: Certain verbs shift their stem vowel specifically in the du and er/sie/es forms, while every other form stays regular. *Fahren* (to drive): *ich fahre, du fährst, er fährt, wir fahren, ihr fahrt, sie fahren* — notice the a becomes ä only in du/er, not elsewhere.

*Sehen* (to see) shows a different vowel shift, e→ie: *ich sehe, du siehst, er sieht, wir sehen, ihr seht, sie sehen*. Other common e→i or e→ie verbs include *sprechen* (to speak) → du sprichst, er spricht, and *essen* (to eat) → du isst, er isst.

sections.heading: Why This Matters for Listening
body: Because the change only appears in the du/er forms, recognizing the pattern helps you understand spoken German faster: hearing *fährst* or *isst* immediately tells you the subject is du or er/sie/es, even without hearing the pronoun clearly.

These stem changes must be memorized verb by verb, but they follow a small number of predictable patterns (a→ä, e→i, e→ie), so learning a handful of common examples makes recognizing new ones far easier.

example.problem: Conjugate 'sprechen' (to speak) for du and er, and use er's form in a sentence: 'He speaks German.'
steps: Sprechen has an e→i stem change in du/er.
du sprichst; er spricht.
Full sentence: Er spricht Deutsch.
example.answer: Er spricht Deutsch (He speaks German), using the stem-changed spricht.

keyTerms.def: A verb whose stem vowel shifts only in the du and er/sie/es forms, like fahren (fährst) or sehen (siehst).
One stem-change pattern, seen in fahren (du fährst) and other verbs.
Another stem-change pattern, seen in sprechen (du sprichst) and sehen (du siehst).
The ich, wir, ihr, and sie/Sie forms of a stem-changing verb, which stay fully regular.

practice.q: What is the 'du' form of 'sehen' (to see)?
practice.explain: Sehen has an e→ie stem change in the du form: du siehst, not the regular du sehst.

practice.q: In which forms does a German stem-changing verb actually change?
practice.explain: The stem-vowel change appears specifically in the du and er/sie/es forms; ich, wir, ihr, and sie/Sie stay regular.

practice.q: What is the 'er' form of 'essen' (to eat)?
practice.explain: Essen has an e→i stem change: er isst, not the regular er esst.

lessons.title: Asking Questions and Negation
lessons.intro: German questions come in exactly two shapes, W-question or yes/no, and negation splits cleanly between two different words depending on what you're negating.

sections.heading: W-Questions and Yes/No Questions
body: W-question words include *wer* (who), *was* (what), *wann* (when), *wo* (where), *wie* (how), *warum* (why). In a W-question, the question word takes first position and the verb stays second, following the normal V2 rule: *Wo wohnst du?* (Where do you live?).
For a yes/no question, simply put the verb first, before the subject: *Sprechen Sie Deutsch?* (Do you speak German?). No extra 'do/does' auxiliary is needed, exactly like Spanish and French.

sections.heading: Nicht vs Kein
body: *Nicht* (not) is the general negator, typically placed near the end of the clause or right before the specific thing being negated: *Ich spreche nicht gut Deutsch* (I don't speak German well). *Kein/keine* (not a/no) specifically negates a noun that would otherwise take ein/eine or no article at all: *Ich habe keinen Hund* (I don't have a dog).

The key test: if the sentence would use *ein/eine* (or nothing) for the noun, negate with *kein/keine*; if you're negating a verb, adjective, or already-definite noun, use *nicht*. *Ich habe einen Hund* → *Ich habe keinen Hund*, but *Ich spreche Deutsch* → *Ich spreche nicht Deutsch*.

example.problem: Say 'I don't have a car' and 'I don't speak German well' in German, choosing nicht or kein correctly.
steps: 'A car' = ein Auto, so negate with kein: Ich habe kein Auto.
'Speak German well' negates the adverb/verb combination, so use nicht: Ich spreche nicht gut Deutsch.
example.answer: Ich habe kein Auto. Ich spreche nicht gut Deutsch.

keyTerms.def: A question starting with a question word (wer, was, wo...), with the verb in second position.
A question formed by placing the verb first, before the subject: Sprechen Sie Deutsch?
The general negator 'not,' used for verbs, adjectives, and definite nouns.
'Not a/no,' used to negate a noun that would otherwise take ein/eine or no article.

practice.q: Which negator fits: 'Ich habe ___ Zeit' (I don't have time)?
practice.explain: Zeit (time) would take no article in the positive, so it's negated with keine (feminine); nicht negates verbs/adjectives, not typically bare nouns like this.

practice.q: How do you form a yes/no question in German?
choices: Put the verb first, before the subject
Only use rising intonation, never word order
practice.explain: German yes/no questions invert to verb-first order: Sprechen Sie Deutsch?, with no auxiliary 'do' needed.

practice.q: Which negator would you use for 'Ich spreche ___ Französisch' (I don't speak French)?
practice.explain: Französisch (a language, used without an article here) is negated with nicht, since you're negating the verb/object combination, not an ein-type noun.

units.title: Food, Shopping, and Directions
units.summary: This unit puts your German to work in three of the most common real-world situations: eating out, buying things, and finding your way around.

lessons.title: Food and Ordering: Mögen and Gern
lessons.intro: German splits 'liking' between two common patterns, mögen for a general liking of a thing and gern for enjoying an activity, and both come up constantly when talking about food.

sections.heading: Mögen: To Like
body: *Mögen* conjugates as: *ich mag, du magst, er/sie/es mag, wir mögen, ihr mögt, sie/Sie mögen*. It's used directly, subject-first, just like English: *Ich mag Pizza* (I like pizza), *Magst du Kaffee?* (Do you like coffee?).
Mögen works well for liking a noun (a food, a person, a thing) but sounds odd applied directly to an activity; for actions, German instead uses gern, covered next.

sections.heading: Gern + Verb
body: To say you enjoy doing something, add *gern* (gladly) after a regular conjugated verb: *Ich esse gern Pizza* (I like eating pizza, literally 'I eat gladly pizza'), *Ich trinke gern Kaffee* (I like drinking coffee). This is the single most common way Germans express enjoying an activity.

Useful food words: *das Brot* (bread), *das Wasser* (water), *das Fleisch* (meat), *das Hähnchen* (chicken), *der Reis* (rice), *das Gemüse* (vegetables), *das Obst* (fruit), *der Kaffee* (coffee). To order politely, say *Ich hätte gern* + item (I would like): *Ich hätte gern das Hähnchen*. To close the meal, ask *Die Rechnung, bitte* (The check, please).

example.problem: Say 'I like eating chicken' and 'I would like the chicken with rice, please.'
steps: 'I like eating chicken' uses gern + verb: Ich esse gern Hähnchen.
'I would like' = Ich hätte gern; add the food and mit Reis (with rice): Ich hätte gern das Hähnchen mit Reis.
Add bitte for politeness.
example.answer: Ich esse gern Hähnchen. Ich hätte gern das Hähnchen mit Reis, bitte.

keyTerms.def: 'To like,' used directly with a noun: ich mag Pizza.
'Gladly' added after a conjugated verb to express enjoying an activity: ich esse gern Pizza.
'I would like,' the polite way to order food.
'The bill/check,' requested at the end of a meal.

practice.q: How do you say 'I like drinking coffee' in German?
practice.explain: Gern follows the conjugated verb to express enjoying an activity: ich trinke gern Kaffee, literally 'I drink gladly coffee.'

practice.q: Which word directly means 'to like' a noun, as in 'ich mag Pizza'?
practice.explain: Mögen is used directly with a liked noun (ich mag Pizza), while gern pairs with a verb to express enjoying an activity.

practice.q: What is the polite way to order food in German?
practice.explain: Ich hätte gern (I would like) is the standard polite ordering phrase, softer than the more direct ich will (I want).

lessons.title: Shopping, Prices, and Comparisons
lessons.intro: A handful of set phrases cover shopping in German, and the comparative system, though it looks different from English at first glance, follows one very consistent rule.

sections.heading: Asking Prices
body: To ask a price, say *Wie viel kostet das?* (How much does this cost?). Describe something as expensive or cheap with *teuer* (expensive) or *billig* (cheap): *Das ist zu teuer* (That's too expensive).
Prices combine directly with numbers and currency: *Das kostet zwanzig Euro* (This costs twenty euros). *Haben Sie etwas Billigeres?* (Do you have something cheaper?) is useful for comparing options.

sections.heading: Making Comparisons
body: German forms the comparative by adding *-er* to the adjective, plus *als* (than): *billiger als* (cheaper than), *teurer als* (more expensive than): *Das ist billiger als das andere* (This is cheaper than the other one). For equality, use *so...wie* (as...as): *Es ist so gut wie das andere* (It's as good as the other one).

Many one-syllable adjectives also add an umlaut in the comparative: *alt* (old) → *älter* (older), *groß* (big) → *größer* (bigger). The superlative adds *am -sten*: *am billigsten* (cheapest), *am größten* (biggest).

example.problem: Say 'This shirt is bigger than that one' in German.
steps: 'Bigger than' = größer als, using the umlaut comparative of groß.
Build the sentence: Dieses Hemd ist größer als das andere.
example.answer: Dieses Hemd ist größer als das andere.

keyTerms.def: 'How much does this cost?' — the standard way to ask a price in German.
The standard comparative construction: adjective + -er + als (than), as in billiger als.
'As...as,' used to express equality between two things.
A comparative that adds an umlaut along with -er, as in alt → älter, groß → größer.

practice.q: How do you say 'This is more expensive than that'?
choices: Das ist mehr teuer als das
Das ist so teuer als das
Das ist teuer mehr als das
practice.explain: German comparatives add -er directly to the adjective, followed by als (than): teurer als.

practice.q: What is the comparative form of 'groß' (big)?
practice.explain: Groß takes an umlaut in the comparative: größer, not a regular grosser.

practice.q: Which phrase expresses that two things are equal?
practice.explain: So...wie means 'as...as,' expressing equality; -er...als expresses inequality (comparative), and am -sten forms the superlative.

lessons.title: Directions and Prepositions of Place
lessons.intro: A short list of direction words gets you from lost to found in any German-speaking city, and the verbs involved are refreshingly simple, formal commands aside.

sections.heading: Giving and Following Directions
body: Key direction words: *rechts* (right), *links* (left), *geradeaus* (straight ahead). *Gehen Sie geradeaus* (Go straight ahead, formal command with Sie) is a common instruction. *Biegen Sie rechts ab* (Turn right) uses the separable verb *abbiegen* (to turn off), where *ab* splits to the end of the clause.

This separable-verb pattern, where a prefix like *ab-* detaches and moves to the end of a main clause, is common in German and worth noticing here even before studying it formally: *abbiegen* becomes *biegen ... ab*.

sections.heading: Prepositions of Place
body: Useful prepositions: *in der Nähe von* (near), *weit von* (far from), *zwischen* (between), *neben* (next to/beside), *gegenüber von* (across from), *hinter* (behind). *Die Bank ist in der Nähe von der Post* (The bank is near the post office).
As with sein covering location generally, these phrases all pair naturally with sein: *Das Museum ist zwischen der Apotheke und der Bank* (The museum is between the pharmacy and the bank).

example.problem: Give directions: 'Go straight, then turn left. The hotel is next to the bank.'
steps: 'Go straight' = Gehen Sie geradeaus (formal command).
'Then turn left' uses the separable verb abbiegen: dann biegen Sie links ab.
'Next to' uses sein + neben: Das Hotel ist neben der Bank.
example.answer: Gehen Sie geradeaus, dann biegen Sie links ab. Das Hotel ist neben der Bank.

keyTerms.def: 'Right' / 'left,' the core direction words.
'To turn (off),' a separable verb whose prefix ab- moves to the end of the clause: biegen Sie ... ab.
'Next to/beside,' one of several prepositions of place.
A German verb whose prefix detaches and moves to the end of a main clause, like abbiegen → biegen ... ab.

practice.q: Where does the 'ab' go in 'Biegen Sie rechts ab' (Turn right)?
choices: To the end of the clause, since abbiegen is a separable verb
It moves to the very front
practice.explain: Abbiegen is a separable verb; its prefix ab- detaches and moves to the end of the main clause: Biegen Sie rechts ab.

practice.q: What does 'gegenüber von' mean?
practice.explain: Gegenüber von means 'across from'; neben means 'next to,' and hinter means 'behind.'

practice.q: Which verb do location and direction phrases naturally pair with in German?
choices: Sein, since it covers location generally
Werden, since location is a change of state
Mögen, since location is a preference
practice.explain: Just as in French, sein alone covers location in German, so place prepositions pair naturally with it.

units.title: Past Tense and Real Conversation
units.summary: The final unit adds the Perfekt tense for talking about completed past events, then pulls everything together into a realistic conversation.

lessons.title: The Perfekt with Haben
lessons.intro: The Perfekt (present perfect) is the tense Germans reach for in everyday spoken conversation to describe a finished past action, far more common in speech than the simple past tense.

sections.heading: Building the Perfekt
body: The Perfekt has two parts: a present-tense form of *haben* (or, for some verbs, sein) plus a past participle placed at the end of the clause. For most verbs, haben is the auxiliary: *ich habe gemacht* (I did/made), *du hast gespielt* (you played), *er hat gelernt* (he learned).

Regular (weak) verbs form their past participle as *ge- + stem + -t*: *machen → gemacht*, *spielen → gespielt*, *lernen → gelernt*. The participle goes to the very end of the clause, after the auxiliary, which sits in the normal V2 verb position.

sections.heading: Strong Verbs with Haben
body: Strong (irregular) verbs often change their stem vowel and take *-en* instead of *-t*: *sehen → gesehen* (ich habe gesehen, I saw/have seen), *essen → gegessen* (ich habe gegessen, I ate), *lesen → gelesen* (ich habe gelesen, I read).
Because these verbs are extremely common, their irregular participles are worth memorizing directly, the same way English speakers just know 'saw/seen' rather than deriving it from a rule.

example.problem: Say 'Yesterday I played soccer and I ate pizza' using the Perfekt with haben.
steps: 'I played' from spielen, regular participle: ich habe gespielt.
'I ate' from essen, irregular participle: ich habe gegessen.
Combine with gestern (yesterday), remembering the participle goes to the end: Gestern habe ich Fußball gespielt und Pizza gegessen.
example.answer: Gestern habe ich Fußball gespielt und Pizza gegessen.

keyTerms.def: The German compound past tense, built from an auxiliary verb (haben or sein) plus a past participle at the end of the clause.
A regular past participle formed as ge- + stem + -t, like gemacht (from machen).
An irregular past participle, often with a vowel change and -en ending, like gesehen (from sehen).
The German rule placing the past participle at the very end of the clause, after the auxiliary in second position.

practice.q: What is the past participle of the regular verb 'lernen' (to learn)?
practice.explain: Regular (weak) verbs form their participle as ge- + stem + -t: lernen → gelernt.

practice.q: What is the past participle of 'essen' (to eat)?
practice.explain: Essen is a strong verb with an irregular participle, gegessen, rather than the regular -t ending.

practice.q: Where does the past participle go in a German main clause?
choices: At the very end of the clause
practice.explain: The past participle is placed at the end of the clause, while the auxiliary (haben/sein) stays in the normal second verb position.

lessons.title: The Perfekt with Sein
lessons.intro: Like French être-verbs, a specific set of German motion and change-of-state verbs use sein instead of haben as their Perfekt auxiliary, and they're some of the most common verbs in the language.

sections.heading: Which Verbs Use Sein
body: Verbs of motion or change of state typically use sein: *gehen* (to go) → *ist gegangen*, *fahren* (to drive/travel) → *ist gefahren*, *kommen* (to come) → *ist gekommen*, *fliegen* (to fly) → *ist geflogen*. *Sein* itself is irregular: *ich bin gewesen* (I was/have been).

*Sie ist nach Berlin gefahren* (She traveled to Berlin) uses sein (ist), not haben, because fahren describes movement from one place to another. Unlike French, German past participles with sein do not change form for the subject's gender or number — gefahren stays gefahren regardless of who traveled.

sections.heading: Recognizing the Pattern
body: A rough test: if the verb describes movement toward a destination, or a change of state (like being born or dying, *geboren*/*gestorben*), it likely takes sein. Verbs describing an action with no inherent destination, like *essen* or *spielen*, take haben instead.

*Ich bin in Berlin geboren* (I was born in Berlin) shows sein used for a change-of-state verb; compare this to *Ich habe in Berlin gewohnt* (I lived in Berlin), which uses haben because wohnen (to reside) describes a state, not a change or directed motion.

example.problem: Say 'Yesterday she went to the store and she came home late' using the Perfekt with sein.
steps: 'She went' from gehen, sein-verb: sie ist gegangen.
'She came' from kommen, sein-verb: sie ist gekommen.
Combine with gestern, zum Geschäft, and spät nach Hause: Gestern ist sie zum Geschäft gegangen und spät nach Hause gekommen.
example.answer: Gestern ist sie zum Geschäft gegangen und spät nach Hause gekommen.

keyTerms.def: A set of motion/change-of-state verbs (gehen, fahren, kommen, and others) that use sein instead of haben in the Perfekt.
Unlike French être-verbs, German sein-verb participles never change form for the subject's gender or number.
A category of sein-verbs including werden (to become), geboren (born), and sterben (to die).
A rough rule: motion toward a destination or change of state takes sein; other actions take haben.

practice.q: Which verb uses sein, not haben, in the Perfekt?
practice.explain: Gehen is a motion verb and takes sein as its auxiliary, unlike regular haben-verbs like spielen, essen, or lernen.

practice.q: Does the past participle 'gefahren' change form based on the subject's gender, as in French?
choices: No, German sein-verb participles never change form
practice.explain: Unlike French, German past participles with sein stay unchanged regardless of the subject's gender or number: gefahren stays gefahren.

practice.q: Which verb category typically takes sein as its Perfekt auxiliary?
choices: Motion toward a destination or change of state
All verbs starting with a vowel
practice.explain: Verbs describing directed motion (gehen, fahren) or change of state (werden, sterben) typically take sein; other actions take haben.

lessons.title: Putting It Together: A Real Conversation
lessons.intro: Every tool from this course, greetings, sein/haben, cases, present tense, mögen, and the Perfekt, comes together in one realistic exchange you could have today.

sections.heading: A Sample Conversation
body: Consider this exchange at a café: *A: Hallo! Wie geht's? B: Mir geht's gut, danke. Und dir? A: Auch gut. Was hast du gestern gemacht? B: Ich bin ins Kino gegangen. Magst du den Film? A: Ja, ich mag ihn sehr.* Notice hast...gemacht and bin...gegangen (Perfekt, one with haben, one with sein) and mag/mag ihn (mögen with an accusative pronoun).

This short exchange draws on nearly every grammar point from this course: greetings, the dative in mir geht's, the Perfekt with both auxiliaries, and mögen with a case-marked pronoun — exactly how real fluency works, weaving multiple structures together rather than using any one rule in isolation.

sections.heading: Building Your Own Exchange
body: A reliable template for a first conversation: greet (Hallo/Guten Tag), ask how someone is (Wie geht's?), ask about a recent event with the Perfekt (Was hast du gemacht?), and react with a mögen-based opinion (Ich mag es / Ich mag es nicht).

From here, expanding your German is mostly a matter of vocabulary, not new grammar structures — the patterns in this course (sein/haben, cases, present tense, Perfekt, questions, negation) cover the large majority of everyday conversation you'll encounter.

example.problem: Write a two-line exchange: ask a friend what they did last weekend, and have them answer that they visited their grandmother and it was very nice.
steps: 'What did you do last weekend' = Was hast du am Wochenende gemacht?
'I visited my grandmother' uses haben + besucht: Ich habe meine Großmutter besucht.
'It was very nice' uses war (the simple past of sein, natural for describing a resulting feeling): Es war sehr schön.
example.answer: A: Was hast du am Wochenende gemacht? B: Ich habe meine Großmutter besucht. Es war sehr schön.

keyTerms.def: 'What did you do?' — the Perfekt question used to ask about a specific past event.
'I like it,' using mögen to react to something, with es as the accusative object.
A reusable pattern of greeting, asking a state, asking about a past event, and reacting, useful for any first exchange.
The principle that real fluency comes from weaving multiple grammar points together, not mastering one rule in isolation.

practice.q: In 'Was hast du gestern gemacht?', which auxiliary is used, and why?
choices: Haben, since machen is a regular action verb, not motion or change of state
Werden, since it's about the future
practice.explain: Machen takes haben as its Perfekt auxiliary since it doesn't describe motion toward a destination or a change of state.

practice.q: Which question asks specifically about a past action?
practice.explain: Was hast du gemacht? uses the Perfekt (hast...gemacht) to ask what someone did in the past; was machst du? asks about the present.

practice.q: According to this lesson, what mostly drives further progress in German after this course?
choices: Vocabulary, since the core grammar patterns are now covered
Learning a completely new grammar system
Abandoning the Perfekt for a simpler tense
practice.explain: The lesson argues that the grammar patterns taught cover most everyday conversation, so vocabulary growth becomes the main driver of further progress.
